subject: Canada's factories only look flat because of prices
bodyMarkdown:
Statistics Canada put out two reports on Friday morning that look dull and are not. If you are waiting to see whether the Bank of Canada hikes again, or you work anywhere near a steel mill or a sawmill, they show you what the Bank will be staring at when October inflation lands on Monday.

## What the factory numbers actually said

The Canadian Press reported on Friday that Statistics Canada found manufacturing sales essentially unchanged in September at $80.2 billion. Flat. Then comes the second line of the release: in **constant dollars**, which strips price changes out to show how much stuff actually got made, sales fell 1.5 per cent. The dollar total held still while real output shrank. Sales dropped in 11 of the 21 subsectors. Petroleum and coal products rose 10 per cent, and the release credits higher prices for much of that gain. I keep coming back to that pairing. The one subsector doing the most to hold the headline up is the one where the increase is mostly price rather than volume. Take it out and September was a down month on the factory floor, dressed up as a quiet one.

## The tariffs show up in metal and wood

Primary metal sales fell 9.5 per cent in September, the steepest drop in the release, and wood products fell 7 per cent. Those are the two corners of Canadian industry sitting directly under the American Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and lumber, and I do not think the timing is an accident. The wholesale report, out the same morning, read better at first glance. Sales excluding petroleum and grain rose 0.7 per cent to $92.5 billion, machinery and equipment climbed 3.6 per cent to $20.7 billion, motor vehicles and parts added 2.4 per cent to $15.5 billion, and the yearly comparison was up 7.8 per cent. In volume terms that same basket slipped 0.2 per cent. Same shape as manufacturing. Dollars up, units down.

## Why this makes the Bank's job harder

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate a quarter point to 2.5 per cent on October 28, its first increase in more than three years, and it moved because energy costs were pushing prices up. BNN Bloomberg reported on Friday that economists expect inflation to stay elevated and are divided on whether energy is bleeding into everything else. Friday's data arms both camps. Anyone who wants a second hike points at petroleum up 10 per cent and wholesale sales up 7.8 per cent from a year ago. Anyone who wants the Bank to sit still points at 1.5 per cent less real factory output, unemployment that Statistics Canada put at 6.7 per cent in October, and a job market that has shed positions three months running. My read is that this is price pressure sitting on top of a weakening economy, which is close to the hardest thing a central bank can be handed.

## The takeaway

Watch Monday's CPI release, and watch the core measures more than the headline figure, because what matters is whether dearer energy has pulled other prices along with it. If you have a mortgage renewal coming in the next year, price it off a 2.5 per cent policy rate that could go up before it comes down. If you work in metals or lumber, that 9.5 per cent is your operating environment and not a line in a table. I would not read Friday's flat headline as stability.
